ctaTitle: Ready to Choose the Right Delivery Method?
ctaText: Let's talk about your project and determine whether Design-Build or traditional construction is the best fit for your goals, timeline, and budget.
content:
There's a moment in every construction project where the owner realizes something.

The architect and the contractor aren't on the same team.

They're on different teams. With different contracts. Different incentives. Different definitions of success.

And when something goes wrong — and something always does — those two teams point at each other while the owner stands between them paying for the delay.

This is not a bug in traditional construction. It's a feature of how it was designed.

Design-Build exists to fix it.

Here's the honest comparison every Florida project owner needs before they choose a delivery method.

How you structure your project team is the decision that determines whether everyone works together — or against each other.

What Is Traditional Construction? (Design-Bid-Build)

Traditional construction — formally called Design-Bid-Build — follows a linear, sequential model.

It works like this:

  • The owner hires an architect to design the project
  • The architect produces completed drawings and specifications
  • The owner solicits bids from general contractors
  • The owner selects a contractor and signs a second contract
  • The contractor builds to the architect's design

Two teams. Two contracts. One owner managing both.

The system has been around for over a century. It's deeply familiar. And for certain project types — publicly funded projects, projects with existing architect relationships, projects where competitive bidding is required — it still makes sense.

But it has structural problems that have never been solved. Only managed.

The Structural Problems of Traditional Construction

The designer and the contractor have never worked together before your project starts.

The architect designs in relative isolation. The contractor sees the drawings for the first time when they submit a bid. Nobody reviews the design for constructability — for whether it can actually be built as specified, on the stated budget, in the available time — until the moment someone is trying to price it.

And by then, the design is done. Changes are expensive.

The Result → Designs that look perfect on paper but cost 20–40% more to build than the owner expected. Scope gaps between what the architect drew and what the contractor priced. Disputes about who is responsible for what. Change orders. Delays. And an owner caught between two parties who each believe they're right.

This is not a criticism of architects or contractors. It's a criticism of a system that puts them in an adversarial position by design.

What Is Design-Build?

Design-Build is a project delivery method where a single entity manages both design coordination and construction under one contract with the owner.

One team. One contract. One point of accountability.

The Design-Build contractor holds contracts with architects, engineers, and all specialty consultants. The owner talks to one team. That team is responsible for the complete outcome — from concept to closeout.

The model doesn't eliminate architects or engineers. It changes who holds the relationship with them.

Instead of the owner managing the architect and the contractor separately — and mediating their conflicts — the Design-Build GC manages the full team. The owner's job becomes setting direction, making decisions at key milestones, and holding one party accountable.

In Design-Build, there is no one to blame but the team you hired. Their only option is to solve the problem.

The Side-by-Side Comparison

Here's how the two methods compare across every dimension that matters to project owners:

FactorDesign-Bid-Build (Traditional)Design-Build
ContractsTwo separate contractsOne single contract
AccountabilitySplit between designer & contractorSingle point — the GC
TimelineLonger — sequential phasesFaster — overlapping phases
Cost ControlDesign locked before budget realityCost input during design
CommunicationOwner manages two teamsOne team, one conversation
Design ChangesExpensive after design is completeManageable during process
DisputesCommon — designer vs contractorRare — same team
Owner WorkloadHigh — constant coordinationLower — GC manages it all
RiskSpread across parties, falls on ownerHeld by Design-Build team
Best ForPublic bidding, existing architect relationshipsSpeed, simplicity, accountability

Where Design-Build Wins — And Why

Speed

In Design-Bid-Build, construction cannot begin until design is fully complete and permits are issued. These phases are strictly sequential.

In Design-Build, design and construction planning overlap. Permits can be submitted for early phases while later phases are still being designed. Long-lead materials can be ordered during design.

The result: Design-Build projects typically complete 10–30% faster than equivalent traditional projects.

In Florida's construction market, where lease obligations, business timelines, and seasonal constraints make schedule critical, this is not a marginal advantage.

Cost Control

Here's the core problem with traditional construction budgeting:

The architect designs. Then the contractor prices it. If the price is too high, the architect redesigns. Then it gets priced again. This cycle — design, price, redesign, reprice — is expensive and demoralizing.

In Design-Build, the contractor's cost expertise is in the room during design. Every significant design decision gets evaluated for its budget impact before it gets committed to drawings. Value engineering is woven into the design process, not bolted on after the fact.

Real Number → According to research from the Design-Build Institute of America, Design-Build projects deliver 6% lower cost growth and are delivered 33% faster than traditional Design-Bid-Build projects. In a Florida commercial build, that cost difference alone can run into six figures.

Accountability

When a traditional construction project has a problem, the first question is always: whose fault is it?

Was it the architect's design? Was it the contractor's execution? Was it a gap in the specifications? Was it a subcontractor the owner didn't even know was on the project?

In Design-Build, this question has one answer. The Design-Build team is responsible. Full stop.

This doesn't mean problems don't happen. It means they get solved instead of litigated.

Communication

On a traditional project, the owner receives information from two sources — the architect and the contractor — who often have different interpretations of the same situation.

On a Design-Build project, one team manages all information. The owner has one point of contact, one source of schedule updates, one phone number to call when something needs attention.

This sounds simple. It changes everything.

Where Traditional Construction Still Makes Sense

Design-Build is not always the right answer. Here's when traditional construction makes more sense:

Publicly funded projects with mandatory competitive bidding

Many government and institutional projects are legally required to use competitive bidding processes. Design-Bid-Build is the standard procurement method for these projects.

When you have an existing architect relationship you want to preserve

If you've worked with a specific architect for years and want to maintain that direct relationship, traditional construction keeps the architect reporting directly to you.

Note: A good Design-Build GC can still work collaboratively with your preferred architect. The structure changes; the relationship doesn't have to.

When maximum design control is the priority

If you want absolute control over every design decision before any construction begins, Design-Bid-Build keeps design authority with you and your architect through the entire design phase.

Honest Perspective → These are legitimate reasons to choose traditional construction. But most private owners, developers, and business owners in Florida who choose Design-Bid-Build do so out of habit or familiarity — not because it's the better model for their project. The data consistently favors Design-Build on cost, schedule, and satisfaction.

The Biggest Misconception About Design-Build

Most owners who haven't used Design-Build assume one thing:

That because the contractor controls the design coordination, design quality suffers.

The opposite is true — when the team is right.

When the people building the project are also coordinating the design, they design for buildability. They know what works in the field. They catch the details that look fine on paper but create problems in construction. They know which specifications are genuinely necessary and which are over-engineered for the actual use case.

A Design-Build GC with strong design coordination capability doesn't reduce design quality. They bring construction reality into the design process.

The key phrase: when the team is right.

Design-Build concentrates accountability. That's its strength. But it also concentrates risk. Choosing the wrong Design-Build firm produces the worst of both worlds — poor design and poor construction — with no clear party to hold accountable.

Vetting the Design-Build team is everything.

Design-Build doesn't guarantee a great project. It guarantees that one team owns the outcome. Whether that's good or bad depends entirely on who that team is.

faqs.q: Is Design-Build more expensive than traditional construction?
faqs.a: Not in total project cost — and often less. While the GC's role is broader in Design-Build, the cost savings from avoided redesigns, faster delivery, and better procurement typically outweigh the additional coordination fee. The Design-Build Institute of America's research consistently shows lower cost growth in Design-Build projects vs. traditional.

faqs.q: Can I use my own architect in a Design-Build project?
faqs.a: Yes. Keentel General Contractors works collaboratively with owner-selected architects and engineers. The structure shifts — the architect coordinates with our team rather than reporting directly to you — but the relationship and the design quality don't have to change.

faqs.q: What is a Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) in Design-Build?
faqs.a: A GMP contract caps your total construction cost. The Design-Build contractor guarantees the project will not exceed the stated maximum. Any savings below the GMP may be shared between owner and contractor depending on contract terms. A GMP is only as reliable as the scope definition it's based on — this is why thorough pre-construction planning matters.

faqs.q: Is Design-Build appropriate for large commercial projects in Florida?
faqs.a: Absolutely. Design-Build is particularly well-suited to larger, more complex projects where subcontractor coordination, schedule management, and cost control are priorities. The larger the project, the more valuable single-team accountability becomes.

faqs.q: How does Design-Build affect permitting timelines in Florida?
faqs.a: Typically positively. Because design and construction planning happen in parallel, permit applications can be submitted earlier in the process. A Design-Build GC with experience in Florida's municipal permitting environments also manages the process more efficiently than an owner coordinating separately between an architect and contractor.

faqs.q: What types of projects are best suited for Design-Build in Florida?
faqs.a: Commercial tenant buildouts, office construction, industrial facilities, warehouse construction, restaurant build-outs, medical offices, facility expansions, and any project where schedule, budget control, and coordination complexity are priorities. Design-Build is less commonly used for simple residential projects or publicly-bid institutional work.
